answer.text: The Korean War began on June 25, 1950, when the North Korean People’s Army launched a surprise invasion across the 38th parallel into South Korea and swiftly captured Seoul.

As the first major test of containment, the war prompted the United States to resist communist expansion while avoiding a wider global conflict, and MacArthur’s proposal to expand hostilities against China intensified debate over those competing goals.

Fear that communism would spread through Asia led the United States to defend South Korea after the invasion, heading a United Nations coalition whose military assistance was authorized by Security Council Resolution 83.

After a military stalemate, fighting stopped under the July 27, 1953 armistice, which created a 2.5-mile-wide fortified DMZ near the 38th parallel but, because it was a truce rather than a peace treaty, left the conflict technically unresolved.
The war killed more than two million Koreans, and its armistice preserved Korea’s division without a formal peace treaty while creating the heavily fortified DMZ that still separates North and South.
China entered to support North Korea against the US-led UN forces because advances toward the Yalu River threatened the collapse of its ally and the loss of North Korea as a protective buffer state.

Truman rejected MacArthur’s proposals to expand the war into China and use nuclear weapons because he sought to prevent a world war, whereas Eisenhower promised an early and honorable end, visited the Korean front, and concluded that negotiations offered the only way out.

I also want to understand its effects on US politics, any major errors that occurred, and how different presidents perceived the conflict.
